**Where we are ahead:** the only Zig option that is not tied to one server (any `router`), secure defaults (`.none`, credentials-with-`*` refused at init, `Vary` always correct on intercepted preflights), a comptime `Static` posture that compiles to header slot writes, and an explicit migration hatch for APIs that stamp `*` on everything; wire output anchored to flask_cors with a judged divergence ledger; audited 2026-09-10. **Where we are behind:** ~~no origin wildcard patterns~~ DONE 2026-10-11 (`Origins.patterns`); ~~no `Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network`~~ DONE 2026-10-11 (`allow_private_network`); ~~no pass-through of preflights to the handler~~ DONE 2026-10-11 (`preflight_passthrough`); no debug logging and no request-aware origin function (`AllowOriginRequestFunc`/`AllowOriginVaryRequestFunc`) — both consciously rejected, reasons in Backlog. rs/cors's `OptionsSuccessStatus` (a status other than 204 for legacy clients) is also not offered (Backlog).

## Design & invariants
- **Immutable, reentrant:** an initialized `Cors` has no clock, no locks, no hidden globals; the
  only allocation is the init-time join of configured lists (freed by `deinit`). The hot path
  reflects borrowed request slices only — safe across all connection threads.
- **Preflight always intercepted:** `OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method` gets 204, no
  body, handler never runs — regardless of origin/route validity. CORS headers appear only when
  origin + requested method + requested headers all pass; a failed preflight is still 204 without
  them. Every intercepted preflight carries `Vary: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method,
  Access-Control-Request-Headers`.
- **Actual requests always continue down the chain:** CORS only withholds the headers that let a
  cross-origin script read the response. Headers set when `Origin` present + allowed and method in
  `allowed_methods`; `.any` emits `*`, a list/predicate match echoes the origin; every actual response of a list/patterns/predicate policy carries `Vary: Origin`, refused or not (rs/cors).
  Origin matching is exact byte compare (or caller predicate) — no normalization; the
  `.patterns` variant adds validated `scheme://*.host[:port]` subdomain patterns (below).
- **Secure default, deliberately not rs/cors's:** `allowed_origins` defaults to `.none` (rs/cors
  defaults to permissive `*`); `allowed_headers` defaults to `.reflect` (matches expressjs).
- **Credentials vs. wildcard rejected at construction:** `Cors.init` rejects `.any` +
  `allow_credentials = true` with `error.CredentialsWithWildcardOrigin` rather than silently
  downgrading; a `.predicate` returning true is the explicit, greppable opt-in.

## Origin patterns, private network, pass-through (parity — rs/cors, 2026-10-11)

**Patterns** (`Origins.patterns = .{ .exact, .subdomains }`). rs/cors splits an `AllowedOrigins` entry at
its first `*` into prefix and suffix and accepts any origin that starts with one, ends with the other and
is at least as long as both (utils.go:12-16, cors.go:181-185), after lowercasing both sides. Taken
literally that grants `https://evil.com/.example.com` and `https://.example.com` for
`https://*.example.com`, and `https://evil.com@a.example.com`. **Ours deliberately differs:** a separate
variant (so `.list` keeps its exact-compare meaning and a stray `*` there is still just a byte), each
pattern validated at `init` (`error.InvalidOriginPattern`: `scheme://*.host[:port]`, the `*` directly
after `://` and before a `.`, at least two host labels after it so `*.com` is refused, all-digit port, no
path/userinfo/second `*`), and the part the `*` covers must be one or more complete labels
(`[a-z0-9_-]+`, single dots between) — so it cannot leave the host. `*` may span dots
(`a.b.example.com` matches, as in rs/cors; a one-label-only mode is a possible tightening, not asked for).
Scheme and port must be equal (the pattern's absent port means the origin has none). Matching is byte-exact,
unlike rs/cors's lowercasing, for the same reason as `.list`. A match is echoed with `Vary: Origin`, so
patterns are legal with credentials; `exact` entries keep the `"null"`/`"*"` credentials rejection.
Per-request cost: one `indexOfScalar` plus prefix/suffix compares per pattern.

**Private Network Access** (`allow_private_network`, rs/cors cors.go:231-232 and 390-392): off by
default; on, the preflight `Vary` gets `, Access-Control-Request-Private-Network` appended (also on a
failed preflight, as rs/cors sets Vary before the gates), and a granted preflight whose request header is
exactly `true` carries `Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network: true` between `Allow-Credentials` and
`Max-Age`. Pinned by a byte golden. Works with `allow_unconditional_wildcard` too.

**Pass-through** (`preflight_passthrough`, rs/cors cors.go:281-285): the middleware writes the preflight
headers (no status), then calls `next`; the handler answers. A failed preflight reaches the handler
headerless. Default unchanged (short-circuit 204).

## Static CORS (deliberate deviation, comptime)

The second named posture, for the same adoption reason as the wildcard one below: a public
read-only API whose grant is a **build-time constant** — one `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value
(`*` or one fixed origin) stamped on every response and every preflight, regardless of `Origin`.
No gates run, and the policy compiles to `setHeaderStatic` slot writes. `Vary` is emitted only on
the one path that genuinely varies: a preflight with `allow_headers = null` echoes the request's
`Access-Control-Request-Headers`, so it carries `Vary: Access-Control-Request-Headers`. Pin
`allow_headers` and the posture is constant end to end and emits no `Vary` at all. Surface: `StaticOptions` + `applyActualStatic` /
`applyPreflightStatic` / `isPreflight` — no `Cors`, no `init`, no allocator. `allow_credentials`
is structurally absent: a constant grant with credentials is the combination `Cors.init` rejects,
so the knob does not exist. First consumer: qap (its `Config.cors` is this type).

## Unconditional wildcard CORS (deliberate deviation, opt-in)

Spec-correct CORS — the default, unchanged — never touches a response the browser isn't asking a
CORS question about: no `Origin` header means no CORS headers, and a plain `OPTIONS` with no
`Access-Control-Request-Method` is not a preflight, it routes normally. That is correct and stays
the default. It is also, on its own, a hard migration wall for one real shape of existing API: one
that has always answered *every* `OPTIONS` with 204 and stamped `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on
*every* response, regardless of `Origin`. Such an API cannot adopt this module without changing what
is on the wire — and "adopting this changes your API's shape" is the most common reason a library
meant for outside consumers doesn't get adopted.

`Options.allow_unconditional_wildcard` (default `false`) is the escape hatch, named so the deviation
is visible at the call site rather than reading like an ordinary feature flag. It requires
`allowed_origins = .any` — enforced at `Cors.init` with `error.UnconditionalWildcardRequiresAnyOrigin`
— because the option's entire meaning is "wildcard on every response"; paired with `.list`/
`.predicate`/`.none` it would have nothing coherent to gate on. When true: `applyActual` sets
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` unconditionally (dropping the `Origin`-presence and
`allowed_methods` gates), and `middlewareRun` intercepts every `OPTIONS`, ACRM or not, through the
same `handlePreflight` path (which itself skips the origin/method/header gates for the same reason).

**One field, not two — the two behaviours (unconditional emission; bare-`OPTIONS` interception) are
bundled deliberately.** They read as independent (a consumer could imagine wanting either alone),
but they are two symptoms of one underlying posture: a legacy CORS gate that never conditioned on
`Origin` in the first place. Splitting them into separate flags would let a consumer enable only
one half and still hit the exact problem the option exists to solve — the wire shape changing for
the *other* kind of request (e.g. unconditional headers on GET/POST but a bare `OPTIONS` still
falling through to a 404/405, or vice versa). One field keeps the migration atomic and keeps the
whole posture a single grep target (`rg allow_unconditional_wildcard`).

## Header timing vs. `ResponseWriter.reset()`

`middlewareRun` calls `applyActual` **before** `next.run` — CORS headers land on the response before
the handler chain executes. That is deliberate, not an oversight: `http.Server.ResponseWriter`
buffers a response until the first body write (or an explicit streaming opt-in) commits the head, and
`setHeader`/`reset` both fail `error.HeadersSent` once that has happened. Moving `applyActual` to
*after* `next.run` (evaluated and rejected — see below) would fail exactly that way for any handler
that streams its body, which `cors` cannot assume no route does.

The consequence: an *outer* middleware that calls `ResponseWriter.reset()` after `next.run` — e.g. to
replace a `text/plain` denial body with JSON — wipes every header `cors` set, `reset` clears the
header list wholesale, and there is no way for `cors` to see that happen or be asked again
automatically. `http.Server.ResponseWriter` has no snapshot/restore and no header-read primitive
(the same gap the `Vary`-clobber hazard above lives on), and that lives in `http`, out of scope here.

**The fix lives entirely inside `cors`: `applyActual` is `pub`.** A response-rewriting middleware
calls `your_cors.applyActual(ctx.req, ctx.res)` again immediately after its own `reset()`, before
writing the new body — the exact same gate, idempotent, safe to call twice. This is documented as
the concrete rule in README.md rather than left as "reapply the headers somehow": the alternative
(the outer middleware reimplementing the origin/method gate itself) would drift the moment `cors`'s
gate logic changes.

**Considered and rejected: swap the ordering (apply after `next.run` instead of before).** This is
the "ordering" fix the task brief flags as worth evaluating. It was rejected because it is not a
pure reordering — it changes what a streaming handler experiences. `next.run`'s completion does not
imply the head is still unsent: a streaming handler (chunked/SSE-style responses) can commit the head
partway through its own body, and `applyActual` running afterward would then return
`error.HeadersSent`, which propagates as an unhandled `anyerror` — a 500 on a route that previously
worked, on *every* request to it, not just ones behind a `reset()`-calling outer middleware. That
regression is strictly worse than the one being fixed (which only bites when a specific pattern of
outer middleware is present) and it cannot be scoped away, since `cors` is deliberately router-agnostic
about what any given handler does. Default ordering stays as-is.

## Threat model / out of scope
CORS is a browser-enforced contract, not a server-side access-control mechanism: it never blocks a
request from executing server-side, only whether a cross-origin script may read the response — must
not be used as an authorization boundary. Exact-byte origin matching means case/trailing-slash/port
mismatches silently fail to match (documented, not a bug); normalization is the caller's job. A
handler that sets `Vary` itself replaces (not merges) the middleware's value — unfixable inside this
module, since `http.Server.ResponseWriter` exposes neither an append (`addSetCookie` is
Set-Cookie-only) nor a way to read a set response header, so there is nothing to merge WITH, before
or after `next`. Consequence: the per-origin `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` ships with a `Vary` that
no longer names `Origin`, which a shared cache can turn into a cross-origin response mix-up; the
caller-side rule is that a handler setting `Vary` on a CORS route lists `Origin` too. Both the
hazard and the safe shape are pinned by a test, so an `http` append primitive would arrive with a
red assertion pointing at the fix. A pass-through preflight (`preflight_passthrough`) is subject to
the same replace-not-merge hazard for its `Vary`. Subdomain patterns grant every subdomain of the
named zone: a dangling or user-controllable subdomain of it (takeover, user-content hosts) is then an
allowed origin, which is the nature of the feature — pattern a zone you control end to end.

## Performance

**Fastest in the field, 2026-10-23** (`zig build bench-cors`). labstack/echo v5.4.2
`middleware.CORS` (`tools/go_fast_bench`) and tower-http 0.7.1 `CorsLayer` over httparse
(`tools/rust_fast_bench`); each side's own `plain` workload is subtracted, so the ratios are net
of the HTTP stacks. Neither contender checks Access-Control-Request-Method or -Headers on a
preflight (less work than ours and rs/cors), tower-http answers it 200 (compared as 204), neither
has the `wildcard` subdomain patterns (that row is rs/cors only). Ours: preflight 1.13–1.23×
tower-http (1.38× before the one-pass header gather, CHANGELOG), actual 0.50×, disallowed 0.56×;
echo is slower than rs/cors on every row. The rest of the preflight cost is the HTTP server's
(parsing the longer head, writing more headers), which tower-http's net pays the same way.

**Re-measured on Zig 0.17.0, 2026-10-20** (`zig build bench-cors`, `BENCH_ROUNDS=5`, same host, ReleaseFast; load average 1–4 from other sessions, largest spread 14.4 %): ref 0.30–0.48×, against 0.23–0.58× on Zig 0.16.0 (Go on the host 1.26.0 → 1.26.8 in between, where Go is a side). The card carries these figures.

## Backlog / deferred
- **No-panic sweep 2026-10-29:** a client-chosen `Origin` (`.predicate`/`.patterns` echo) or reflected `Access-Control-Request-Headers` could exhaust the 4 KiB header-copy store and make a later `setHeader` fail → 500 with the handler skipped (CO-1; R2-1 from the independent review: the "fits but leaves too little" band). Fixed at the root: every value cors owns is stored by `setHeaderStatic`/`setHeaderBorrowed` (no copy budget); only request echoes copy, and a failed echo is no grant / an omitted ACRH. Configured CR/LF/NUL values panic at init in every mode (were Debug-only asserts; release failed each matching response). Reports: `~/CML/20261029-panic-sweep/cors-sweep.report.md`, `review-aaa-gate-cors.report.md`.
- ~~**`Vary: Origin` missing on actual responses without an allowed Origin**~~ — DONE 2026-10-20: every actual response of a `.list`/`.patterns`/`.predicate` policy carries `Vary: Origin` (granted, refused, no Origin, failed method gate), as rs/cors's `handleActualRequest` ("Always set Vary"); `.any` and `.none` do not vary. Browser-oracle answers re-taken (74 refusal answers gained the field, 504 fetches still agree with Chrome).


- ~~**Origin patterns with a subdomain wildcard**~~ DONE 2026-10-11 — `Origins.patterns` (see "Origin patterns, private network, pass-through").
- ~~**`Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network`**~~ DONE 2026-10-11 — `allow_private_network`.
- ~~**Preflight pass-through option**~~ DONE 2026-10-11 — `preflight_passthrough`.
- **Debug logging** (rs/cors `Debug`/`Logger`) — rejected: the hot path does no I/O and has no logger dependency; the three pure gates are public, so a caller that wants to log a decision does so around them.
- **Request-aware origin function** (rs/cors `AllowOriginRequestFunc`, `AllowOriginVaryRequestFunc`) — rejected for now: the existing `.predicate` sees only the origin string. A decision that depends on other request headers needs those names added to `Vary` (rs/cors needed a second function type for exactly that), the gates are deliberately request-type-free (`allowOriginValue` is pure), and a caller can already decide per request outside the middleware and call `applyActual`/`applyPreflight` directly. Revisit when a consumer has a tenant-by-`Host` case.
- **`OptionsSuccessStatus`** (rs/cors, default 204; a few legacy clients choke on 204) — not offered: no consumer, and the pass-through lets a handler pick any status. Effort: tiny if asked (one `u16` option).
- **Single-label `*`** — a pattern mode where `*` may not span dots. Not asked for; rs/cors spans.

## Status
`gap · any · util · reentrant` + deps: `router`, `http` — canonical source is `pub const meta` in
src/root.zig.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — every path's expected values come from an implementation that is not ours.

**What the tests actually contain.** src/browser_oracle_test.zig replays headless Google Chrome 155 (`tools/interop.zig` + `tools/browser_oracle.js`, frozen 2026-10-05, re-taken 2026-10-20 for the `Vary` change below): `fetch()` from two page origins against the middleware under 16 gated configurations (list / any / none origins, method sets, reflected and listed headers, credentials, expose lists incl. `*`, max-age, `allow_unconditional_wildcard`, a list entry with a trailing slash and one with an upper-case scheme) and the 2 static-posture ones, 14 request shapes each (simple GET/POST/HEAD, preflighted PUT/DELETE/PATCH and `patch`, custom headers, JSON `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, credentialed) -- 504 fetches. Chrome's verdict (a response or a network error; could the script read `X-Total` / `X-Secret`) must equal the configured policy, the Fetch Standard's CORS checks applied to the configuration in the driver; and the middleware must still answer every request Chrome sent with the head Chrome judged (status, every `Access-Control-*` and `Vary` field, in order). the `interop (flask_cors oracle)` tests in src/root.zig keep the earlier flask_cors 6.0.5 comparison with its 8-item divergence ledger. Not judged by a browser: `Vary` and `Access-Control-Max-Age` (caching, which no fetch verdict shows -- their bytes are pinned by the replay), the `predicate` origin form (caller code), and the opaque `null` origin.

**How it got there.** DONE 9dee82e: flask_cors oracle; its wildcard+credentials default is the unsafe one. 2026-10-05: the browser oracle. It found two places where the module's answer and the browser's reading of it parted: a preflight for `patch` (which `fetch()` does not upper-case) was granted with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: ..., PATCH`, which Chrome refuses -- methods now compare byte for byte (RFC 9110); a listed header name with surrounding spaces (`" X-A"`) matched nothing although the browser reads the joined list with the spaces stripped -- configured names are now trimmed.
